blocks.html:
I’ve been really into what gnuhr has been doing for about two or three years now. Honestly, I get thrilled every time they put something new out because it’s always so interesting to see what they come up with. I wanted to take some time today to actually talk about it.


I’ve always been willing to do Nur Abbas’ work, and I’m a huge fan of his history, specifically his time at Nike with ACG. I’ll be talking more about him later in a separate post to understand where he is now and how his work at ACG changed how I see the brand. But for now, I wanted to dedicate this space to gnuhr specifically.


What I really appreciate about gnuhr is how they manage to create technical garments that stay easy to read. There’s a strong sense of coherence in every piece. Nothing feels random, and nothing is there just to call attention for the sake of it. The details, the shapes, and the materials are all exactly where they need to be. gnuhr doesn’t try to impress you with flashy effects; it impresses with intention.

That’s especially true when you look at how innovative they are. A lot of what I’ve talked about here was based on products from a couple of years ago, but even today they just put out the warp tee tank. It’s a tee using really specific materials, and the coolest part is that you can actually customize it. There are about 45 different configurations for the bust, the length, the sleeve length, and the neck. You can really work around the configuration to create what you need. You can make it a tank top, or keep the sleeves like a baseline tee and get it really cropped.


This is where I think fashion could be more thrilling and more open to people. Right now, most brands follow the path of standard measurements. They build clothes for a specific size, which is how things work in the West, but it doesn’t fit everyone perfectly. gnuhr is building a way for people to get an almost perfect fit. Today, if I want a piece of clothing that is actually perfect for me, I usually have to find someone to cut and sew it specifically for my body. gnuhr is bringing that kind of precision to the brand itself. It’s also mainly made in Italy. I know the way of working in Europe isn’t always perfect, but I really trust gnuhr on that part because we haven’t seen anything go wrong with their quality.

I’ve always been drawn to well-designed clothing, the kind where you can actually feel the reasoning behind the construction and the logic behind every seam. But often I get disappointed because so many brands lose themselves in their own complexity. gnuhr is the opposite. There’s clarity. You understand what you’re wearing and why it’s built that way.


What I love is that when I buy something from gnuhr, it actually makes me want to go outside and put it to the test in the conditions it was meant for. I really appreciate it when a brand is about more than just selling a piece of fabric or a lifestyle. It’s about how to enjoy being outside, how to enjoy trying different environments and really exploring. I see Nike do this a lot of the time, and even with ACG they are sometimes quite good with certain pieces, but for gnuhr, it isn’t the branding or the marketing that makes me want to go out. It’s the design. It’s how the clothes look and the feeling you get that they actually thought about it. They felt like, “Okay, in this type of environment, when you’re cold and exhausted, this specific fabric and this specific style will make you feel good.” It’s about getting the message through the technicality of the garment. I feel like they really do that perfectly.


I also really like the attention they put into their visuals. The photos they use are always great, and they do these cool photo albums on their website when they go to specific destinations to test new equipment. It’s really cool because it gives you a real place where to use those pieces. They call these trip reports, and they often share their own feelings and descriptions of the trip, which is awesome. It shows the real-world application of what they are building.

There’s also something about the way they present themselves. Sometimes they do things that feel a bit “silly,” and I think it almost wakes up that childish part of us. You know, that same childish part that just wants you to go explore. I love that they can balance being so technical while still tapping into that sense of wonder.


I’m also really into how they embrace lightness. Over the last few years, the textile world pushed this idea that heavier means more serious or more technical. But that weight just tires you out. It holds you down and disconnects you from your movement. gnuhr does the opposite. Lightness isn’t a lack of something; it’s a deliberate decision. It’s a way of saying that performance should follow you, not weigh on you.


I really feel that when I wear their stuff. It’s comfortable, it gives me room, and it moves with me. It’s not there to impress anyone; it’s there to work. The brand’s message is clear: you don’t need to overdo it. It just needs to work and be right.


That mindset shows in their fabric choices too. gnuhr uses highly technical textiles, the kind you’d expect in alpine gear, like Dyneema for its strength-to-weight ratio and Polartec Alpha for thermal breathability. These aren’t just marketing moves. They’re deliberate, functional decisions that show real respect for performance and the person actually wearing the clothes.

Beyond that, I really like how they handle collaborations. They’ve made some very smart moves by working with others, and I love how smaller or medium-sized minds find ways to share ideas and work together. If you like discovering new brands, it’s always really interesting. It’s almost like a stamp on the brand; it says, “This is who we follow, and you should too.” It’s really something special.


It’s refreshing to see a brand treat design as research in a moment where so much outdoor gear has turned purely decorative.
